# Harbor Coordination Papers -- Critique Ledger

Purpose: the complete inventory of every actionable item raised in the review memoranda on the
Harbor coordination papers, so "did we go through all of this" becomes a query against this
table (filter by `Status`) instead of a memory someone has to hold. Extraction only -- rows
record what a reviewer said, not whether it is right; no row implies agreement.
Id scheme: `#` is `<PREFIX>-<NNN>`, one prefix per source document below (`HAH`, `RT`, `PD`,
`RP`, `PP`, `CPR`, `XS` for the exposition-review corpus, `LR` for the outside
literature review, `CA` for the Critical Analysis of 2026-09-08), numbered in the order the item
appears in its source. Ids are permanent -- never renumber or reuse one; retire a row via
`Status` instead.
Current edit authority is `docs/harbor-research/omni-ledger.json`, field
`critique_rows`. Add or update a row there, retaining its permanent ID. Run
`python3 scripts/harbor-research/omni_ledger.py render` to regenerate the JSON
projection, then `python3 scripts/harbor-research/render_critique_ledger.py` to
refresh this consolidated table and `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_critique_ledger.py`
to validate it. The renderer refuses independently edited projection rows;
review those edits and transfer them deliberately to Omni before regenerating.
`Status` and `Notes` are left blank throughout for the author to fill in (`Status` values:
empty, `DONE <sha-or-PR>`, `IN-WAVE-<n>`, `DECLINED -- <reason>`, or `BLOCKED -- <branch>`).
`BLOCKED` is for a row whose fix is real and agreed but whose file another branch owns, so it
can be neither landed nor declined from here; it counts as open, never as closed, and it names
the branch so the row is a routing instruction rather than a shrug. The rule the four values
exist to enforce is that `Status` is the field a reader queries, so it must never disagree with
`Notes` -- a `DONE` whose own evidence refutes it (as `CA-045` carried for a while) is worse
than an empty cell, because an empty cell at least does not lie.
See `docs/harbor-research/LIBRARY-SYSTEM.md` (forthcoming) for how this ledger fits the
broader research-library workflow.

### 3.3 SHEAF STATISTICAL-HARNESS AUTOPSY (todo W8's real content; the working minimal proof is sheaf_mechanism_proof.py; the broken wrapper is wrong-turns/sheaf_verdict.py)
**Symptom:** in the wrapper (docs/harbor-research/wrong-turns/sheaf_verdict.py), full-visibility scenario showed 0 redundant detections (should be ~200: pairwise must fire when an equivocator perturbs compared edges) and 0 cohomology-only detections everywhere — coh signal wasn't tracking injected inconsistency at all.
**Diagnosed defects (in my head only until now):**
- **D1 — restriction maps kill coker.** Per-edge random orthonormal S×D projections (S=3, D=6) make the coboundary δ generically SURJECTIVE once edges are plentiful ⇒ coker(δ)=0 ⇒ harmonic space empty ⇒ signal ≡ 0 regardless of data. The scalar minimal case works precisely because identity restrictions give coker = cycle space. **Fix:** restrictions must be coordinate-subset selections (shared-prefix coordinates), or scalar/low-d stalks, so coker(δ) ≅ (cycle space) ⊗ (shared coords) and carries the cocycle constraints.
- **D2 — masking applied inconsistently.** `pairwise` was computed from the FULL disagreement cochain g (before removing uncompared edges) in some paths, and the coh signal never modeled the uncompared entries as unknown — it projected a g that silently contained the "hidden" edge's value. **Fix:** compute g only on compared edges; treat uncompared blocks as free variables.
- **D3 — wrong detector under partition.** The correct statistic when some edges are unobserved: does ANY completion of the unknown entries make g a coboundary? i.e. residual r = min over (x, free blocks) of ‖g_known − (δx)|_known‖; equivalently, project the known-edge vector onto the orthogonal complement of {(δx) restricted to known edges}. r > 0 ⟺ cocycle obstruction visible from the observed edges alone. (On a cut edge the free block absorbs everything ⇒ r = 0 always — which is exactly the honest boundary, now falling out of the algebra.)
**Rebuild spec:** stalks ℝ^d, restriction = selection of shared coordinates per edge; equivocator = per-neighbor offset vectors on its reports (so around any cycle through it, offsets don't cancel); observed g on compared edges only; detector = the least-squares completion residual r; localization = support of the minimizing residual vector; baseline = pairwise on compared edges; run two_path (two bridges ⇒ severed bridge lies on a cycle) vs single_bridge (cut edge), 200 trials, plus expander with random uncompared edges. Success gate unchanged from the assessment: cohomology-only detections in partition-on-a-cycle; ~0 on cut edges; redundant under full visibility. Expected counting caveat: net out topological β₁ per lesson #2.

## 9. WHAT TO DO NEXT — written 2026-09-08, for whoever picks this up cold

Four things landed today that are only half-useful until somebody else uses
them. Each one is written here as a job with a first command, because the
failure mode for all four is the same: they sit there, correct and unread, and
the next agent solves the problem they already solve.

### 9.1 `pd roadmap push` exists now. Somebody has to run it, on a schedule.

`lib/roadmap-mirror-push.ts` + `pd roadmap push` fill the relay's roadmap mirror
(`apps/relay/src/roadmap-mirror.ts`, migration `2026-08-22-roadmap-mirror.sql`,
applied in staging). That mirror shipped in August as "PR 1 of 4" and **nothing
ever pushed to it** — PR 2 was never written — so it was a well-tested empty
table for a fortnight, and every reader built since went and found the roadmap
somewhere else instead. That is the shape of failure to watch for here: the
storage is convincing enough that people assume the pipeline exists.

The job: run it on `git:committed`, the way `scripts/export-roadmap-snapshot.ts`
was always meant to be run — its own docstring names "a `pd-fleet.yml`
Cartographer trigger" as the intended automation and nobody built that either.
Same trigger, both verbs.

    pd roadmap push --dry-run          # prints source, item count, bytes, age
    pd roadmap push                    # needs `pd account login` first

**The one invariant not to break.** `generatedAt` is the DAEMON's clock and it
travels with the data, so a fallback push of a fortnight-old committed snapshot
arrives in the mirror reading as a fortnight old. Re-stamping it with
`Date.now()` is a one-character "fix" that turns the only staleness signal the
mirror has into a lie. Two tests in `tests/unit/roadmap-mirror-push.test.js`
hold that line; if one of them ever looks like an obstacle, it is not.

### 9.2 The Work Register is PR 3 of 4. Say so, and finish it.

`apps/relay/src/work-register.ts` now reads `roadmap_mirror_items` rather than a
`work_registry_cache` of its own (that table and its meta table are gone, along
with the GitHub round trip and the `refresh` verb, which answers 410 with the
command). The register was built beside the roadmap programme without either
knowing about the other; now they share a table, and the honest move is to stop
treating them as two projects. `docs/reports/relay-roadmap-mirror/MANIFEST.md`
says the board pages were PR 3 — the register IS those pages.

What is left:
- The site surface. The author asked for "an API only my account can talk to,
  and a web viewer only I can see". The mirror is account-scoped, so that is
  already the shape; `/register?repo=owner/name` is the page.
- The limitation, which is written into `2026-09-08-work-register.sql` where the
  deleted tables used to be: claims are per-repository and shared, the registry
  half is per-account. One operator with many agents is one set. Two operators
  are not. Do not "fix" this by reaching around the mirror's tenancy rule —
  `apps/relay/tests/roadmap-mirror.test.ts` asserts a cross-account read is a
  404 and that assertion is correct.

### 9.3 `\ifpdbook` is the tool for every Book/paper divergence from here on.

Declared in `figures/pd-hyperlinks.tex` (false), set true in the Book preamble
immediately after that file loads. Not a two-argument macro — the generator
inlines every `\input`, so a figure branch is a whole table environment and a
macro argument is scanned as one token list whether or not it is used. Not
guarded with `\ifdefined` either: a conditional token inside skipped text counts
as a nested `\if` and desynchronises `\fi` matching. Ordering is cheaper than
cleverness, and the three failed attempts are written out in commit `76d18bf82`
so nobody has to rediscover them.

Use it whenever a chapter and its standalone twin should say different things.
The next instance is already known: `thm:fh-escrow-bound` is stated in BOTH
chapter 6 and chapter 8 under two numbers, and `check_duplicate_figures.py`
catches duplicated drawings but nothing catches a duplicated theorem.

**Whoever generalises that checker: read only the `\ifpdbook` branch**, the way
`check_duplicate_figures.py` already does, with a scanner rather than a regex —
the branches contain prose and nested `\ifnum` from other macros.

### 9.4 One D1 test adapter, and it earned its keep in ten minutes.

`apps/relay/tests/helpers/d1-sqlite.ts` is now the only D1-over-`node:sqlite`
adapter; `roadmap-mirror.test.ts`'s `makeRealDb` delegates to it. Use
`applyAllMigrations()`, not `migration('one-file.sql')`. A suite that loads a
single migration is testing a schema that has never existed anywhere: the table
is there but the foreign keys pointing at the rest of the database are not, so a
constraint that bites in production cannot bite in the test. Switching the
register's surface suite over immediately caught two rows production would have
refused — a `users` insert with no `github_user_id` and no `created_at`, and a
`work_board_members` row pointing at a user id that did not exist — both of
which had been passing green.

round trip:

- Chapter 6 stopped re-inputting drawings chapters 7 and 8 develop. True, and it

**no edit to a twin source may change the standalone paper's figure count.**

# The Harbor library: how it is built, checked, and edited

This is the canonical description of the research library behind *The Harbor, the
Person, and the Economy*. The twin-location headers in the `.tex` sources, the index
README, and the critique ledger all point here; this file changes slowly, the index
and the ledger change often.

## 1. What the library is

The library is one argument published in two forms and one book.

- **The Book** (`website-v2/public/whitepaper/coordination-papers-mega-volume.tex`, the
  textbook edition) is generated by `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs` from eight
  chapter sources and one source of record, `whitepaper/textbook.json`, which fixes
  chapter order, numbering, the four parts, edition metadata, and each chapter's question
  and epigraph. Nothing else states a chapter number.
- **The eight chapters** are the standalone whitepapers under `whitepaper/` and
  `website-v2/public/whitepaper/`; each compiles on its own and declares only its
  `\pdchapterprefix`.
- **The seven research papers** (`docs/harbor-research/tex/paper1.tex` through
  `paper7.tex`) are submission-form write-ups of the executed results R1 to R17, CR, and
  B6. They are byte-stable artifacts: the Book folds their content into chapter prose,
  and the papers do not change except for the twin-location header comment.

**The twin-location rule.** Every result that lives in a paper and in a chapter carries
the same header comment in both files, naming the other file, the sections involved, the
index ids, the three commands that check them, and this document. If a number or a
statement changes in one location it must change in the other in the same commit;
`check_library_index.py` fails the build otherwise.

## 2. The reference index

`docs/harbor-research/library-index.json` is the inverted index: for every result id
(R1 to R17, CR, B6, and folded propositions), its one-breath statement, its standalone
home, its chapter locations, the figures and scripts that back it, the key numbers with
regexes that must match at every location, the mechanization rows, and the site anchors.
`library-index.schema.json` is its shape; `library-index.README.md` explains every field
and how to add an entry; `LIBRARY-INDEX.md` is the generated human-readable render and is
never hand-edited.

The checker, `scripts/harbor-research/check_library_index.py`, enforces: (a) every listed
label and anchor exists; (b) every theorem-family label and environment in the three
corpora is claimed or explicitly allow-listed, and every theorem environment carries a
label; (c) every key number matches, by regex, at the standalone and at every chapter
location; (d) both files of a folded pair carry the twin header and name each other;
(e) each chapter's declared prefix agrees with `textbook.json`; (f) `LIBRARY-INDEX.md` is
fresh (`--write-md` regenerates it, `--check-md` fails on staleness). Its unit tests live in
`tests/harbor-research/`.

## 3. The figure system

Figures are drawn in TikZ to one house grammar (`docs/harbor-research/figures/CONVENTION.md`
and `figures/pd-figure-language.tex`) in the semantic palette of `figures/pd-palette.tex`,
whose light values are held in lockstep with the website's tokens by
`website-v2/scripts/check-figure-palette.mjs`. Every folded result gets exactly two
figures in the program grammar: a relation map for its analogy and a regime diagram for
its boundary. The `harbor-chartwork` skill (`skills/harbor-chartwork/`) holds the diagram
taxonomy, the craft rules, the sourced research notes, and the mechanical QA: a
source-level lint for TikZ fragments, a fragment compiler, a rendered-PDF checker for
overflow, overlap, and dead canvas, and a contact-sheet builder for before-and-after
review. Art plates for the Book (cover, frontispiece, part and chapter openers) are
documented in `website-v2/public/whitepaper/plates/README.md` with full provenance.

## 4. The proof and provenance system

Claims are labeled by kind: **Theorem** (follows from a stated model), **Design
invariant** (intended; backed by implementation and tests), **Model-checked property**
(proved for a bounded or abstract model), **Empirical hypothesis** (needs measurement).
Runtime claims name an assurance mode: Observed, Coordinated, Brokered, Confined, or
Attested. Every number in prose is tagged `[verified]` (recomputable from a closed form or
the literature) or `[internal, script]` (regenerates from a named script and seed; the
program seed is 20260816).

What runs in continuous integration today (`.github/workflows/proofs.yml`):

| Claim | Mechanization | Files | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claim-signaling incentive compatibility, δ* threshold | Z3, TLC, Apalache | `proofs/economics/` | Z3 / delta-threshold; TLA+ / claim-signaling; TLA+ / claim_signaling (Apalache) |
| Bond-ledger conservation | TLC | `proofs/bonded/conservation/Conservation.tla` | TLA+ / bonded Conservation |
| Threat bands | Monte Carlo | `threat-bands.mjs` | Monte Carlo / threat-bands |
| R1 to R17, CR, B6 headline numbers | Python result scripts, seeded | `skills/harbor-results/scripts/` | Harbor results / R-scripts (seed 20260816) |

The ProVerif models under `analyses/` and `proofs/**`, the three Kani
harnesses in `core/harbor-card-rs/src/lib.rs`, and the relay TLA+ configurations run in
continuous integration: `proofs.yml` runs every ProVerif model against its committed
results (`scripts/proofs/run-proverif.py`, with the negative controls asserted to fail),
the fast Kani harnesses on every pull request and the parser harness nightly, the relay
TLA+ specifications with their attack configurations, and the claim-signaling game with
its delta 0.30 counterexample as a negative control. `whitepaper/corpus.json` (schema
`whitepaper/corpus.schema.json`, checker `scripts/check-whitepaper-corpus.mjs`) is the
one manifest: every formal artifact is WIRED or RETIRED, an on-disk artifact missing
from it fails the check, and the Book's Mechanized-claims appendix is generated from
it. Prose about those artifacts states the bounded truth: the Kani harnesses are
no-panic checks on bounded inputs with the cryptography stubbed plus two concrete
attenuation vectors; the every-hop attenuation property is ProVerif's.

## 6. Build and publish

The published PDFs are built by `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh` inside a pinned TeX Live
container (`.github/workflows/whitepaper-build.yml`); a same-repository push or pull
request that changes any TeX input, `textbook.json`, the generator, or the plates makes the
workflow rebuild only the affected papers and commit them as
`build(whitepaper): regenerate PDFs from source`. The research papers have the same loop
in `harbor-research-build`. After a bot commit, run `npm run fix:whitepaper-metadata` in
`website-v2` to resync the catalog's page counts and sizes and the digest manifest, and
push. A run that lands in `action_required` is re-run from the Actions tab.

Locally, a stock Debian/Ubuntu TeX Live compiles every chapter and the Book — all three
editions — from the same sources, in about ninety seconds per edition; the setup is one
apt command plus one fontconfig drop-in, written down in the "Local TeX Live" section of
`skills/harbor-chartwork/SKILL.md`. `tectonic` is still the figure toolchain's reference
engine and `compile_fragment.sh` prefers it when it is on `PATH`, falling back to
`latexmk -xelatex` when it is not. Neither local path downloads packages: a missing `.sty`
is a hard error, not a fetch. CI's pinned image remains the authority for bytes, page
counts and digests — apt TeX Live 2023 and tectonic's bundle break pages differently, so a
local render is evidence about geometry, never about a published page number.

## 7. Editing playbook

The running state of the Textbook Edition build (what has landed, the context budgets for the remaining waves, the token meter, and how to resume) is kept in `docs/harbor-research/exposition/TEXTBOOK-BUILD-LEDGER.md`; update it in the same commit as any wave.

1. Change a result where it lives. If it is folded, change both twins in one commit and
   update the key numbers in `library-index.json`.
2. Run the five library checks in section 5 before pushing; run the chartwork lint and
   fragment compiler for any figure you touched.
3. If you added a theorem, label it, add it to the index or to `unindexed_allow` with a
   reason, and give it a relation map and a regime figure if it is a folded result.
4. If you answered a review item, set its `Status` in `docs/harbor-research/CRITIQUE-LEDGER.md`
   (`DONE <sha>`, `IN-WAVE-<n>`, or `DECLINED -- <reason>`) and run the ledger checker.
5. Never state a chapter number in prose; use `\pdchapref{prefix}{Title}`.
6. Push, wait for the regeneration commit, resync metadata, push again.

## 8. Numbering concordance

The research papers and earlier printings cite chapters by first-edition Roman numerals.
The textbook edition orders chapters by what they stand on.

| First edition | Textbook edition | Prefix | Chapter | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| II | 1 | `swk` | The Single-Writer Kernel | `whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex` |
| V | 2 | `anchor` | The Anchor Protocol | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/anchor-protocol-whitepaper.tex` |
| -- | 3 | `sealed` | The Sealed Harbor | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/sealed-harbor.tex` |
| I | 4 | `ls` | The Legible Swarm | `whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex` |
| III | 5 | `stp` | From Spawn to Person | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/spawn-to-person.tex` |
| IV | 6 | `he` | The Harbor Economy | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/harbor-economy.tex` |
| VI | 7 | `bonded` | The Bonded Commons | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex` |
| VII | 8 | `fh` | The Federated Harbor | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/federated-harbor-whitepaper.tex` |

The Sealed Harbor has no first-edition numeral: it did not exist as a chapter in
the first printing. Its standalone twin is `docs/harbor-research/tex/paper4.tex`
(R9, R10, R11), added to the Book in Wave 4 of the Textbook Edition.

# Harbor Research (session codification, 2026-08-16)
Start at `HANDOFF.md` — repo map, crosswalk of all results, 13 paste-ready wave prompts (W1–W13), and the knowledge dump (§3: citations, toolchain pins, the sheaf-harness autopsy, novelty anchors, numeric master table, environment traps).
The three companion skills live in `skills/{harbor-exposition,harbor-results,falsification-first}` — read those SKILL.md files before doing anything.
Build: `make figures` regenerates the PNGs from `skills/harbor-results/scripts/` (seed 20260816); `make docs` compiles the PDFs from `tex/`. Binaries are deliberately not committed.

After applying this patch, run `npm run skills:sync` so every agent runtime discovers the three skills (symlinks into `.claude/skills`, `.codex/skills`, `.gemini/*`, `.cursor/skills`, `.agy`, `.agents` — gitignored, environment-local; auto-discovery, no registration). Add `-- --scope user` (or run `pd setup`) to install account-wide into `~/.claude/skills`. CI's `skills:sync:check` and `check:skill-mirrors` are unaffected: mirrors are only for skills declaring `metadata.mirrors`, which these deliberately do not.

Rendered artifacts are committed: `pdf/` holds the nine analysis documents (four synthesis docs, three execution reports, the review, the portfolio) and `figures/` the three result figures. `make docs` rebuilds the PDFs from `tex/` using the committed figures; `make figures` re-runs the underlying experiments from `skills/harbor-results/scripts/` (slow — the A7 sweep takes minutes) and overwrites `figures/`.

# Whitepaper source-tree consolidation — plan, not execution

**Status: plan only. No move happens in this PR.** `claude/retire-chapter-pdfs`
is mid-flight on `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh`,
`website-v2/src/data/whitePapers.ts`, and
`website-v2/scripts/check-whitepaper-metadata.ts` — the exact three files a
source move would touch first. Landing a tree move now guarantees a rebase
collision on all three. This document is the inventory and the sequencing so
that whoever executes the move (after `retire-chapter-pdfs` lands) does not
have to re-derive it from scratch.

Every count below was measured against the tree at the time of writing
(`find`, `diff -rq`, `du`, and reading the actual consumer source) — none of
it is estimated.

## 1. The inventory: what lives where

### `whitepaper/` (752 KB)

```
whitepaper/.gitignore
whitepaper/corpus.json                    # formal-artifact / research-program manifest
whitepaper/corpus.schema.json
whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex              # chapter source
whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex       # chapter source
whitepaper/standalone-figures.json
whitepaper/textbook.json                  # THE single TOC source (chapters, parts, slugs)
whitepaper/textbook.schema.json
whitepaper/figures/*.tex                  # 27 files
whitepaper/figures/src/legible-swarm-specialization.py
```

2 chapter `.tex`, 27 figure `.tex` fragments, 1 Python figure source, plus the
JSON registry pair (`corpus.json`/`.schema.json`) and the textbook registry
pair (`textbook.json`/`.schema.json`).

### `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` (64 MB after this PR's deletion, was 93 MB)

```
website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.tex                      # 15 files (top level)
website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures/*.tex               # 58 files
website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.pdf                        # 8 committed PDFs
website-v2/public/whitepaper/plates/**                    # cover/chapter/marginalia art
website-v2/public/whitepaper/art/collected-volume/        # REMOVED by this PR
website-v2/public/whitepaper/publication-digests.json      # SHA-256/pages/bytes per PDF
website-v2/public/whitepaper/manifesto.html
```

The 15 top-level `.tex`: 6 chapter sources (`agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex`,
`anchor-protocol-whitepaper.tex`, `federated-harbor-whitepaper.tex`,
`harbor-economy.tex`, `sealed-harbor.tex`, `spawn-to-person.tex`), the 8
`coordination-papers-mega-volume*.tex` fragments (the collected-volume driver
plus its `-appendices`/`-maritime`/`-preamble`/`-seams`/`-swiss`/
`-swiss-plates`/`-technical` parts), and `margin-apparatus-fixture.tex`.

**This entire directory is served to the internet as static files** — every
`.tex`, every plate `.jpg`, the manifesto — because it lives under
`website-v2/public/`, which Vite copies byte-for-byte into the deployed site.

### Not a mirror: `diff -rq` on the two figure directories

```
$ diff -rq whitepaper/figures website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures | wc -l
76
```

76 diff lines, almost entirely "Only in `website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures`:
`<file>`" — i.e. files that exist in one tree and not the other. This is one
figure corpus that got arbitrarily split across two directories, not two
copies of the same corpus. A consolidation is a **merge**, not a
de-duplication.

### The two source trees combine to 8 chapters, 4 parts

`node scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs /tmp/x` reads `whitepaper/textbook.json`
and reports `generated 8 chapters in 4 parts` — chapters spread across both
trees by `\input` path, driven entirely by the textbook registry, not by which
directory a chapter's `.tex` happens to sit in.

## 2. The twin files — measured, not guessed

Two independent enforcement mechanisms hold pieces of these trees in lockstep.
**They enforce different sets of files. A consolidation that only satisfies
one of them will pass one check and silently break the other.**

### 2a. Auto-synced (drift-checked, `--sync-shared` rewrites them)

From `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs`:

```js
const sharedMapTargets = [
  'whitepaper/figures/pd-textbook-map.tex',
  'website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures/pd-textbook-map.tex',
];
const siteTextbookMirror = 'website-v2/src/data/textbook.json'; // mirrors whitepaper/textbook.json
```

`node scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs --check-shared` (run in
`library-checks.yml`) fails if either `pd-textbook-map.tex` copy drifts from
the other, or if `website-v2/src/data/textbook.json` is missing or stale
against `whitepaper/textbook.json`. `--sync-shared` regenerates both from the
one source of truth (`whitepaper/textbook.json` plus the rendered map).

### 2b. Hard-asserted, NOT auto-synced (a manual edit that forgets the twin breaks the test)

From `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.test.mjs`, line 190:

```js
test('the shared palette and hyperlink files are byte-identical in both source trees', () => {
  for (const name of ['pd-palette.tex', 'pd-hyperlinks.tex', 'pd-figure-language.tex', 'pd-pedagogy.tex']) {
    assert.equal(
      readFileSync(resolve(`whitepaper/figures/${name}`), 'utf8'),
      readFileSync(resolve(`website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures/${name}`), 'utf8'),
    );
  }
});
```

**Four files, not two.** The task brief that prompted this plan named only
`pd-pedagogy.tex` and `pd-figure-language.tex`; the actual assertion also
covers `pd-palette.tex` and `pd-hyperlinks.tex`. All four must stay
byte-identical across whichever new layout is chosen, or
`node --test scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.test.mjs` (wired into
`library-checks.yml`) goes red. There is no `--fix` for this one — it is a
plain `assert.equal`, so the fix is either keep two copies in lockstep by
hand, or consolidate to one copy under a scheme where a single relative
`\input{figures/pd-pedagogy}` resolves from both chapter locations (see §4).

### 2c. A third, unrelated "twin" — do not conflate

`scripts/harbor-research/check_library_index.py`'s `check_twin_headers`
(the "twin-header checker") enforces a **different** twin relationship:
a whitepaper chapter that has "folded" a standalone research paper's theorem
must carry a `TWIN-LOCATION NOTICE` comment naming that paper and its
`docs/harbor-research/library-index.json` entry id. This has nothing to do
with the two-source-tree duplication in §2a/§2b — it links
`whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex` and `whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex` (the
only two chapters currently inside `whitepaper/` proper) to papers under
`docs/harbor-research/tex/`. It is listed here because it is a real consumer
of the **exact path string** `whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex` /
`whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex`:

```
$ grep -c '"file": "whitepaper/' docs/harbor-research/library-index.json
27
```

27 occurrences. Moving either chapter file requires a matching edit to all 27
entries in `docs/harbor-research/library-index.json`, or `check (a) existence`
and `check (d) twin header` in `check_library_index.py` go red.

## 3. Every consumer of these paths (measured)

| Consumer | What it reads | Path assumption that would break |
|---|---|---|
| `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh` | `whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex`, `whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex`; writes PDFs to `$PUB=website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.pdf` | Hard-codes `whitepaper` and `website-v2/public/whitepaper` as two distinct roots (`paper_sources "whitepaper" "..."`) |
| `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs` | `whitepaper/textbook.json` (`textbookPath`), `whitepaper/figures/pd-cite-shortforms.tex` (`loadCiteShortforms` default), `sharedMapTargets`, `siteTextbookMirror` | All four constants above are literal path strings |
| `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.test.mjs`, `scripts/generate-mega-mechanized.test.mjs` | The 4 byte-identical figure files (§2b) plus everything the generator touches | The `assert.equal` in §2b reads both literal paths every run |
| `website-v2/scripts/check-whitepaper-metadata.ts` | `website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.pdf`, `publication-digests.json`, `website-v2/src/data/whitePapers.ts` | `publicDir` resolution and the `pdfPath` → on-disk-file mapping |
| `website-v2/src/data/whitePapers.ts` | `./textbook.json` mirror (§2a); every entry's `pdfPath: '/whitepaper/<file>.pdf'` | The web-absolute `/whitepaper/...` URLs assume `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` is the PDF's directory — Vite serves `public/` at the site root |
| `scripts/harbor-research/check_citations.py` | Scans 3 corpora by glob: `docs/harbor-research/tex/*.tex` (19), `whitepaper/*.tex` (2), `website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.tex` (15) | The three corpus globs are literal in the script header |
| `scripts/harbor-research/check_library_index.py` | `docs/harbor-research/library-index.json` against the two `whitepaper/*.tex` chapter files (§2c) | 27 `"file"` entries per §2c |
| The wider `scripts/harbor-research/check_*.py` family (`check_duplicate_figures`, `check_figure_register`, `check_marginalia_sidecars`, `check_maritime_gold_ink`, `check_plate_provenance`, `check_propagated_corrections`, `check_research_program`, `check_standalone_figures`, `check_tex_environments`) and the `build_*`/`promote_*`/`star_exercise_pointers.py`/`render_figure_audit.py` scripts | Various figure/plate/citation paths under both trees | Each has its own path assumptions; a mover must grep each individually before relying on a green run — this plan does not claim to have audited every one's internals, only that they exist and touch these trees |
| `.github/workflows/library-checks.yml` | Path-triggers on **both** `whitepaper/**` and `website-v2/public/whitepaper/**` explicitly (separate glob lines); runs `--check-shared`, the node test suite, `check_citations.py`, `check_maritime_gold_ink.py`, `check_propagated_corrections.py`, `check-figure-palette.mjs` | Two separate trigger globs; a merged tree needs one glob, not two |
| `.github/workflows/whitepaper-build.yml` | Path-triggers on `website-v2/public/whitepaper/**/*.tex` **and** `whitepaper/**/*.tex` as two separate lines; runs `run_pdf_checks.py` | Same two-glob pattern |
| `.github/workflows/whitepaper-metadata.yml` | Path-triggers on `website-v2/public/whitepaper/**`; runs `test:whitepaper-metadata`, figure-palette, `whitePapers.test.ts` | Single glob, only the public tree |
| `.github/workflows/proofs.yml` | Path-triggers include the **single literal file** `website-v2/public/whitepaper/agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex` (not a glob) | A rename of this one file silently drops it out of the proofs trigger unless the workflow is edited in the same commit |
| `.github/workflows/harbor-research-build.yml` | `docs/harbor-research/tex/**`, unrelated to the two whitepaper trees directly but shares the citation/library-index machinery | No direct path dependency on `whitepaper/` or `website-v2/public/whitepaper/`, listed for completeness since it runs the same `make -C docs/harbor-research docs` pipeline |
| The website build (Vite) | Everything under `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` is copied verbatim to the deployed site root at `/whitepaper/...` | Any path under `public/` is a public URL; moving files out of `public/` un-publishes them (correct for `.tex` sources, which arguably should not be served at all — see §5) |

## 4. Proposed single home, and why

**Move everything into `whitepaper/`** (not `website-v2/public/whitepaper/`),
and have `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh` copy only the *build output* — the
committed PDFs, `publication-digests.json`, and the `plates/` art the reader
page displays — into `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` as a generated
publish step, the same way it already writes PDFs there today.

Reasoning:

- `website-v2/public/` is a **web-serving directory**. Every `.tex` currently
  under it is being served to the internet as a static text file with no
  reader use — nobody fetches `/whitepaper/spawn-to-person.tex` from a
  browser. LaTeX source has no business in a `public/` tree; only the
  compiled artifacts (PDF, plate images, the digest manifest) do.
- `whitepaper/` is already the tree that owns the single source of truth
  (`textbook.json`) that both the generator and the site's mirror
  (`website-v2/src/data/textbook.json`) read from. Consolidating source
  *into* the directory that already owns the registry is the smaller
  conceptual move — the registry does not need to move to meet its sources
  halfway.
- This makes `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh`'s existing `$PUB=website-v2/public/whitepaper`
  variable describe exactly what it should always have meant: a *publish
  target*, written only by the build, never hand-edited. Today it is
  simultaneously a source directory (chapters, figures) and a publish
  target (PDFs), which is the actual "mess nobody can name" the cleanup
  request pointed at.

### What does NOT move

- The 8 committed PDFs, `publication-digests.json`, and `plates/**` stay
  under `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` — they are the served artifacts,
  correctly placed.
- `website-v2/src/data/whitePapers.ts` and its `textbook.json` mirror stay in
  `website-v2/src/` — TypeScript only sees `website-v2/src/**`
  (`siteTextbookMirror`'s own comment says so), so the mirror mechanism in
  §2a is not itself something to consolidate away, only to keep pointed at
  the new single `whitepaper/textbook.json` location (unchanged, since
  `whitepaper/` is not moving).

## 5. Ordered move sequence, with the check that must pass after each step

Do not batch these. Each step is small enough to bisect if a check goes red.

1. **Wait for `claude/retire-chapter-pdfs` to land** and rebase this work on
   top of it. Re-diff `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh`,
   `website-v2/src/data/whitePapers.ts`, and
   `website-v2/scripts/check-whitepaper-metadata.ts` against the post-merge
   `main` before starting — that PR is expected to change exactly these
   files.
2. **Move the 58 figure `.tex` fragments** (and `render_montecarlo.py`, the 3
   `.pdf` figure includes) from `website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures/` into
   `whitepaper/figures/`, resolving the 76-line `diff -rq` overlap by hand
   (files present in both keep the `whitepaper/figures/` copy as canonical;
   files present only in one side simply move). Do this BEFORE moving any
   chapter `.tex`, so every chapter's `\input{figures/...}` keeps resolving.
   **Check:** `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_duplicate_figures.py` and
   `check_standalone_figures.py` — both must report zero new duplicates or
   orphans.
3. **Update the four byte-identical files (§2b) to exist once**, at
   `whitepaper/figures/{pd-palette,pd-hyperlinks,pd-figure-language,pd-pedagogy}.tex`,
   and rewrite the `scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.test.mjs` assertion from
   an equality check between two files to an existence check on the one file
   (or, if standalone chapter builds still need the file to physically
   resolve from a second relative root, add that root to the pair
   `sharedMapTargets` tracks instead of deleting the second copy — **do not
   delete the second copy without first proving no standalone `pdflatex`
   build depends on finding it at that relative path**; that is exactly the
   "naive consolidation" this plan was asked to warn against).
   **Check:** `node --test scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.test.mjs`.
4. **Move the 6 chapter `.tex` files**
   (`agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex`, `anchor-protocol-whitepaper.tex`,
   `federated-harbor-whitepaper.tex`, `harbor-economy.tex`,
   `sealed-harbor.tex`, `spawn-to-person.tex`) and the 8
   `coordination-papers-mega-volume*.tex` fragments from
   `website-v2/public/whitepaper/` into `whitepaper/`.
   **Check:** `node scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs /tmp/x` still prints
   `8 chapters in 4 parts`.
5. **Update `scripts/build-whitepapers.sh`** so its `paper_sources` calls read
   every chapter from `whitepaper/` and it writes PDFs to
   `website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.pdf` as before (this becomes purely a
   publish step, per §4).
   **Check:** run the script locally; diff the regenerated PDFs' page counts
   and SHA-256 against `publication-digests.json` (expect a legitimate digest
   update from the source move's line-ending/whitespace normalization, if
   any — verify byte-for-byte content is otherwise unchanged).
6. **Update `docs/harbor-research/library-index.json`**'s 27 `"file":
   "whitepaper/..."` entries only if the chapter *filenames* changed during
   the move (they should not, per this plan — only their directory does, and
   `whitepaper/legible-swarm.tex` / `whitepaper/single-writer-kernel.tex`
   were already inside `whitepaper/` and are not moving). If a future
   revision of this plan also relocates those two files, this step becomes
   mandatory.
   **Check:** `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_library_index.py` — all
   5 checks (existence, coverage, drift, twin header, chapter prefix) at 0
   failures.
7. **Update `scripts/harbor-research/check_citations.py`**'s corpus glob list
   from `[docs/harbor-research/tex/*.tex, whitepaper/*.tex,
   website-v2/public/whitepaper/*.tex]` to the merged single glob.
   **Check:** `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_citations.py` — 0
   orphaned bibitems, 0 dangling cites (same as today).
8. **Update the CI path triggers**: collapse the two-glob pattern in
   `library-checks.yml` and `whitepaper-build.yml` to the single
   `whitepaper/**` glob, and rename the literal
   `website-v2/public/whitepaper/agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex` line in
   `proofs.yml` to its new path.
   **Check:** open a throwaway PR touching only a chapter file and confirm
   all three workflows still trigger.
9. **Update `website-v2/scripts/check-whitepaper-metadata.ts`** if its
   `publicDir`/source-resolution logic assumed chapter `.tex` lived beside
   the PDFs (verify by reading it post-`retire-chapter-pdfs`, since that PR
   is actively editing this exact file).
   **Check:** `npx tsx website-v2/scripts/check-whitepaper-metadata.ts`
   (check-only mode).
10. **Full regression pass**: `node scripts/check-doc-citations.mjs --all`,
    `node scripts/generate-mega-whitepaper.mjs /tmp/x`,
    `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_citations.py`,
    `python3 scripts/harbor-research/check_library_index.py`,
    `cd website-v2 && npx tsc --noEmit && npm test`, and a full
    `npm run build` with a grep of the build output for any now-404 asset
    path (a missing `public/` asset does not fail a Vite build).

## 6. Open question this plan does not resolve

Whether `whitepaper/figures/src/legible-swarm-specialization.py` and
`website-v2/public/whitepaper/figures/render_montecarlo.py` are themselves
part of the "one corpus" or belong in `scripts/whitepaper-plates/` alongside
the other figure-rendering Python (`swiss_prompts.py`, `plates_pipeline.py`)
is a judgment call for whoever executes this move, not a fact this plan
measured. Flag it to the author before step 2.

PAGE 1
 What Cycle Consistency Can Prove About Agent
                    Reports
      A Feature-Specific Observability Audit for Multi-Agent Workflows

                       Erich Owens   erich@curiositech.ai
                                  Curiositech AI Research

                 September 2026; revised after adversarial review



                                     Abstract

      A graph of agent reports can support a precise consistency check, but the check says less
     than a claim of coordination truth. For one integer-valued feature, one observation water-
     mark, and edge-specific endpoint reports, we study whether the resulting edge differences
      could arise from a single value at each agent. We give an exact spanning-forest test and a
     computable failure-separation criterion for a declared feature map and failure library. We
      prove three limits: a forest cannot detect any edge-difference contradiction; gradient-shaped
       errors and consistently false reports pass; and, when the endpoint reports are available, a
      simpler duplicate-claim check detects every cycle inconsistency. An exhaustive, deterministic
      small-graph benchmark exercises these limits and keeps independent ledger truth separate
     from algebraic compatibility. A residual-signature margin states exactly when a chosen
      family of report faults can be told apart; edge connectivity gives an exact support limit
       for arbitrary-amplitude sparse report faults, and a restricted singular-value score quantifies
       their robustness. This paper therefore proposes a narrow audit protocol and a falsifiable
      integration path for agent workflows. It does not establish causal fault localization, an op-
      timal repair controller, or field utility. Earlier versions claimed those results; the claims are
     withdrawn here.

1  Question and contribution

Agent workflows contain claims about work completed, artifacts reviewed, and approvals issued.
An auditor may receive reports over several communication edges and ask whether they are
mutually compatible. This is useful only if the feature, time, and evidence source are fixed. A
numerical score that combines code coverage, visual polish, approval status, and token spend
has no common additive semantics. Likewise, reports from different log watermarks need not
agree even when every participant is honest.
  We examine a concrete candidate feature: the integer count of accepted WorkIntent com-
pletion events for a named work item at one event-log watermark. This feature is an example
schema, not an assertion that existing Port Daddy traces already provide the required edge-
specific observations. Our contribution is an audit of the proposed detector and its information
requirements, plus an explicit observability criterion for selecting typed features and redundant
evidence paths. The graph mathematics is established work, especially in combinatorial Hodge
analysis of pairwise data [2]; cellular sheaves have also been used for network communication
and multi-agent coordination [3, 4, 5]. We do not claim that applying those tools to agent
reports invents a new cohomology theory.
   The useful engineering question is whether the graph check catches a failure that a cheaper
evidence check misses. We make that comparison explicit. A real deployment would addition-
ally require authentic provenance, complete packet collection, a common watermark, and an
independent event ledger. None is supplied by a self-reported LLM score.


                                         1

PAGE 2
2  Typed observation model

Let G = (V, E) be a finite oriented multigraph. Every edge e = (u, v) represents one indepen-
dently collected report packet. Let f name one exact feature schema and w one immutable
event-log watermark. The packet carries endpoint claims ae,u and ae,v in Z, a work-item iden-
tifier, a packet identifier, and a reference to the underlying evidence.  It also carries its fea-
ture/schema version, watermark, and event-log root. Orientation is canonical and fixed before
observations are read. The reported difference is

                                         ye = ae,v −ae,u.                                     (1)

A precheck rejects a missing packet, duplicate packet identifier, mixed feature or schema, in-
consistent watermark, or inconsistent log root. These are input validity failures, not topological
alarms. A packet identifier or hash alone is not proof that an agent, workflow, or ledger produced
a claim. The offline benchmark tests metadata equality and does not verify signatures.
Definition 1 (Compatible edge differences). A complete, metadata-valid observation y ∈ZE is
compatible when there is an x ∈ZV such that ye = xv −xu for every oriented edge e = (u, v).
Compatibility asserts the existence of one node value per agent for this feature and watermark.
It does not assert that x equals the event ledger or that any event really happened.

7  Operational application and scope

A useful production path starts with a typed evidence contract, not with a Laplacian. For each
work item, choose one discrete feature such as accepted completion count. Bind each packet
to the exact work item, schema version, event-log watermark and root, agent identities, packet
identifier, and evidence references.  Verify provenance with the workflow or ledger authority.
Reject incomplete or mixed snapshots. Compare repeated endpoint claims, then compare each
accepted claim with an independent event ledger when authorized. Use graph cycle checks only
where the acquisition or disclosure contract supplies edge differences but withholds the raw
endpoint claims, or where the graph structure is itself an explicit audit target.
   This protocol applies to countable, independently defined facts. It does not automatically
apply to semantic judgments such as code quality or whether a review was persuasive. A hash
requires equality or a cryptographic proof, not arithmetic in R. Safety properties such as “an
unapproved commit was never merged” require event ordering and authorization evidence; a zero
graph residual neither proves nor refutes them. Human intervention should follow provenance
and policy evidence, not an energy ratio or minimum-cut label.
   The prior web and native visualizers illustrate a graph and its derived values. They do not
constitute empirical validation. The prior “real-agent” scripts recorded self-reported scores and
Dirichlet disagreement. Those traces may motivate an interface, but they cannot be counted as
observations for the detector defined here. We preserve this distinction so that later real-data
collection can be judged against an explicit contract.

8  Related work and novelty boundary

Sparse recovery over graph incidence matrices already relates recovery conditions to graph
cycles and girth [1]; our cut-space support criterion is a dual, model-specific graph fact, not
a claimed new sparse-recovery theorem.  Combinatorial Hodge ranking already decomposes
pairwise edge data into gradient, curl, and harmonic parts and uses least squares to measure
cyclic inconsistency [2].  Discourse sheaves model selective communication, including lying,
with sheaf Laplacians [3]. Heterogeneous multi-agent coordination with cellular sheaves and
distributed optimization is developed by Hanks and colleagues [4]; learned sheaf-constrained
coordination appears in Sheaf-ADMM [5]. These sources rule out a general novelty claim for
sheaf-based multi-agent coordination, Hodge triage, or distributed repair.
   The narrower prospective contribution here is a domain-specific evaluation contract: exact
feature and watermark selection, provenance requirements, an independent truth oracle, and a
cheap-baseline cut gate for agent-workflow claims. The mathematics makes the limits of that
contract explicit. Whether an edge-only version has useful sensitivity or lower cost in a real
deployment remains open. We would treat a negative field result as a reason to ship ordinary
typed evidence checks instead.

9  Conclusion

Cycle consistency is a valid and efficiently decidable property of a selected set of edge reports. It
is not a certificate of truthful work, a causal diagnosis, a safety proof, or an optimal repair plan.
In the fully visible endpoint-packet setting, the duplicate-claim baseline catches every cycle
inconsistency and sometimes more. The near-term engineering result is a sharper observability
contract, a computable failure-separation margin for declared interventions, and a reproducible
falsification fixture. A claim of broad utility needs real evidence-grounded traces and a baseline
advantage that this model does not provide.

1  Question and contribution

Agent workflows distribute evidence across roles: an author records work, a reviewer sees a
subset, a CI job observes a commit and test run, and a publisher sees an approval or artifact
receipt. A global claim can fail even when each observed overlap appears locally coherent.
The question is which incompatibilities can be inferred from the evidence an auditor actually
receives.
    Cellular sheaves give a precise language for this question. A stalk records one typed feature at
a cell; restriction maps state which part of a role’s state can be compared on a handoff or joint
contract. Cohomology distinguishes a local face-relation violation from a globally nontrivial
closed obstruction, while relative cohomology tests extension through a visibility boundary.
These constructions are established mathematics [2, 1, 6]. The contribution here is a concrete
agent-evidence contract, exact failure-observability criteria, and an executable comparison with
simpler checks. We make no claim that a topological signature alone establishes which agent
erred.

log watermark. A production observation must bind each packet to its schema, work item,
source identity, log root, and evidence reference. An artifact digest or approval cannot be
treated as a real coordinate merely to make a Laplacian run. We keep the external truth oracle
separate from algebraic compatibility and use a synthetic fixture to expose the information
boundary before collecting field traces.

8  Operational application and scope

A field audit should start from one immutable work item, PR head, workflow attempt, artifact
identity, and ledger watermark. The additive coordinates in the typed fixture can count accepted
completions and validated handoffs. Reviewer approvals, commit digests, and publisher grants
remain exact symbolic predicates checked against authenticated event records. Each edge packet
must say which role acquired it, from which independent source, and through which map its
value enters the stalk. A three-party face contract needs its own provenance-bound receipt if
it is to add evidence; the algebraic face relation alone only changes the interpretation of an
existing edge residual.
   The practical comparison uses the same available inputs for every method: metadata and
provenance checks, repeated-claim equality, an exact typed-constraint solver, and the sheaf

independently extracted ledger or symbolic contract oracle supplies truth labels. A graph or
sheaf score earns an operational claim only  if it improves detection or audit cost at a fixed
false-alarm budget, or gives a measured explanation benefit that a direct solver does not. The
synthetic fixture makes no such field claim.
   Relative cohomology adds a precise question when evidence is partial: can the visible com-
patible section extend through the declared hidden contracts? A nonzero connecting class rules
out any extension under those maps; a zero class leaves actual hidden work unverified. Hodge
components similarly describe the selected cochain complex. Human intervention must follow
authenticated provenance and policy evidence, not a harmonic-to-curl ratio. Large sheaves may
also make exhaustive support-distance and singular-value calculations expensive; deployment
would need bounded, receipted approximations or a smaller audit subcomplex.

9  Related work and novelty boundary

Cellular sheaves, their cohomology, relative exact sequences, and Hodge Laplacians are estab-
lished [1, 2].  Combinatorial Hodge ranking already separates gradient, curl, and harmonic
components of pairwise data [6]. Sheaf cosystolic expansion supplies local-to-global and testing
criteria under strong complex and sheaf hypotheses [3]; it does not make a nontrivial H1 class
visible to a face-only test. Relative spectral diagnostics with a separate grounding morphism
provide another relevant construction [4]. Sparse recovery and coding-distance arguments also
predate the edge-group support theorem [5]. Discourse sheaves model selective communication
and lying [7], while cellular-sheaf coordination has been studied for heterogeneous multi-agent
systems [8, 9].
   The mathematical statements in this paper specialize that literature to a declared agent-
evidence contract. The potentially distinctive contribution is a testable design method: specify
typed and provenance-bound restrictions, compute local, global, and relative obstruction classes,
state exactly which injected report errors the map can distinguish, and compare against an
equal-information direct solver. The heterogeneous fixture demonstrates the method and its
limits; it is not evidence of broad field utility. A useful next result would show that independently
sourced edge and face receipts reveal a real workflow failure more cheaply or more clearly than
direct authenticated contract checks, under a predeclared acquisition and privacy budget.

10  Conclusion

Typed cellular sheaves can express information that a scalar graph cannot: different overlaps
reveal different coordinates, joint contracts impose face relations, and incomplete visibility cre-
ates an extension problem. In the exact fixture, a count-face violation and a closed handoff-loop
obstruction occupy orthogonal cohomological channels; the relative class identifies a visible sec-
tion that cannot extend. The sheaf edge-group distance states when sparse erroneous reports
are detectable or uniquely recoverable. These are precise statements about a selected evidence
complex. The same calculations show why topology alone cannot establish truth: coherent
false reports remain invisible, a face without new evidence cannot increase detection, and a
direct solver with the same packets has the same compatibility information. The field ques-
tion is whether a provenance-bound sheaf audit improves the cost or clarity of checking real
multi-agent work. The protocol here makes that question falsifiable.

                                     Abstract

      A graph of agent reports can support a precise consistency check, but the check says less
     than a claim of coordination truth. For one integer-valued feature, one observation water-
     mark, and edge-specific endpoint reports, we study whether the resulting edge differences
      could arise from a single value at each agent. We give an exact spanning-forest test and a
     computable failure-separation criterion for a declared feature map and failure library. We
      prove three limits: a forest cannot detect any edge-difference contradiction; gradient-shaped
       errors and consistently false reports pass; and, when the endpoint reports are available, a
      simpler duplicate-claim check detects every cycle inconsistency. An exhaustive, deterministic
      small-graph benchmark exercises these limits and keeps independent ledger truth separate
     from algebraic compatibility. A residual-signature margin states exactly when a chosen fam-
        ily of report faults can be told apart, and a Gram-matrix score states the corresponding rank
      condition for continuous fault coordinates. This paper therefore proposes a narrow audit
      protocol and a falsifiable integration path for agent workflows. It does not establish causal
       fault localization, an optimal repair controller, or field utility. Earlier versions claimed those
       results; the claims are withdrawn here.

1  Question and contribution

Agent workflows contain claims about work completed, artifacts reviewed, and approvals issued.
An auditor may receive reports over several communication edges and ask whether they are
mutually compatible. This is useful only if the feature, time, and evidence source are fixed. A
numerical score that combines code coverage, visual polish, approval status, and token spend
has no common additive semantics. Likewise, reports from different log watermarks need not
agree even when every participant is honest.
  We examine a concrete candidate feature: the integer count of accepted WorkIntent com-
pletion events for a named work item at one event-log watermark. This feature is an example
schema, not an assertion that existing Port Daddy traces already provide the required edge-
specific observations. Our contribution is an audit of the proposed detector and its information
requirements, plus an explicit observability criterion for selecting typed features and redundant
evidence paths. The graph mathematics is established work, especially in combinatorial Hodge
analysis of pairwise data [1]; cellular sheaves have also been used for network communication
and multi-agent coordination [2, 3, 4]. We do not claim that applying those tools to agent
reports invents a new cohomology theory.
   The useful engineering question is whether the graph check catches a failure that a cheaper
evidence check misses. We make that comparison explicit. A real deployment would addition-
ally require authentic provenance, complete packet collection, a common watermark, and an
independent event ledger. None is supplied by a self-reported LLM score.

Here B+ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The exact decision r = 0 needs no floating-point

Theorem 1 (Exact cycle test). For a complete integer observation on G, the following are
equivalent: (i) the reports are compatible; (ii) the oriented sum of y around every graph cycle
is zero; (iii) a spanning-forest propagation assigns integer potentials to vertices and every re-
maining edge agrees with its endpoint difference; and (iv) r(y) = 0. The dimension of the real
cycle space is |E| −|V | + c, where c is the number of connected components, including isolated
vertices.

Proof. If y = Bx, each cycle sum telescopes to zero. Choose one root per component, set its
potential to zero, and propagate along a spanning tree by adding or subtracting each oriented
edge value.  Every vertex receives an integer value. A non-tree edge closes a fundamental
cycle, so its agreement with the propagated difference is equivalent to that cycle sum being
zero. Fundamental cycles span the cycle space, proving the reverse implication. Orthogonal
decomposition gives RE = im B ⊕ker BT and hence the equivalence with r = 0.  Finally
rank B = |V | −c and rank-nullity yields dim ker BT = |E| −|V | + c.

7  Operational application and scope

A useful production path starts with a typed evidence contract, not with a Laplacian. For each
work item, choose one discrete feature such as accepted completion count. Bind each packet
to the exact work item, schema version, event-log watermark and root, agent identities, packet
identifier, and evidence references.  Verify provenance with the workflow or ledger authority.
Reject incomplete or mixed snapshots. Compare repeated endpoint claims, then compare each
accepted claim with an independent event ledger when authorized. Use graph cycle checks only
where the acquisition or disclosure contract supplies edge differences but withholds the raw
endpoint claims, or where the graph structure is itself an explicit audit target.
   This protocol applies to countable, independently defined facts. It does not automatically
apply to semantic judgments such as code quality or whether a review was persuasive. A hash
requires equality or a cryptographic proof, not arithmetic in R. Safety properties such as “an
unapproved commit was never merged” require event ordering and authorization evidence; a zero
graph residual neither proves nor refutes them. Human intervention should follow provenance
and policy evidence, not an energy ratio or minimum-cut label.
   The prior web and native visualizers illustrate a graph and its derived values. They do not
constitute empirical validation. The prior “real-agent” scripts recorded self-reported scores and
Dirichlet disagreement. Those traces may motivate an interface, but they cannot be counted as
observations for the detector defined here. We preserve this distinction so that later real-data
collection can be judged against an explicit contract.

8  Related work and novelty boundary

Combinatorial Hodge ranking already decomposes pairwise edge data into gradient, curl, and
harmonic parts and uses least squares to measure cyclic inconsistency [1]. Discourse sheaves
model selective communication, including lying, with sheaf Laplacians [2]. Heterogeneous multi-
agent coordination with cellular sheaves and distributed optimization is developed by Hanks
and colleagues [3]; learned sheaf-constrained coordination appears in Sheaf-ADMM [4]. These
sources rule out a general novelty claim for sheaf-based multi-agent coordination, Hodge triage,
or distributed repair.
   The narrower prospective contribution here is a domain-specific evaluation contract: exact
feature and watermark selection, provenance requirements, an independent truth oracle, and a
cheap-baseline cut gate for agent-workflow claims. The mathematics makes the limits of that
contract explicit. Whether an edge-only version has useful sensitivity or lower cost in a real
deployment remains open. We would treat a negative field result as a reason to ship ordinary
typed evidence checks instead.

9  Conclusion

Cycle consistency is a valid and efficiently decidable property of a selected set of edge reports. It
is not a certificate of truthful work, a causal diagnosis, a safety proof, or an optimal repair plan.
In the fully visible endpoint-packet setting, the duplicate-claim baseline catches every cycle
inconsistency and sometimes more. The near-term engineering result is a sharper observability
contract, a computable failure-separation margin for declared interventions, and a reproducible
falsification fixture. A claim of broad utility needs real evidence-grounded traces and a baseline
advantage that this model does not provide.

Agent workflows contain claims about work completed, artifacts reviewed, and approvals issued.

agree even when every participant is honest.

evidence paths. The graph mathematics is established work, especially in combinatorial Hodge
analysis of pairwise data [2]; cellular sheaves have also been used for network communication

reports invents a new cohomology theory.

evidence check misses. We make that comparison explicit. A real deployment would addition-

7  Operational application and scope

A useful production path starts with a typed evidence contract, not with a Laplacian. For each
work item, choose one discrete feature such as accepted completion count. Bind each packet
to the exact work item, schema version, event-log watermark and root, agent identities, packet
identifier, and evidence references.  Verify provenance with the workflow or ledger authority.
Reject incomplete or mixed snapshots. Compare repeated endpoint claims, then compare each
accepted claim with an independent event ledger when authorized. Use graph cycle checks only
where the acquisition or disclosure contract supplies edge differences but withholds the raw
endpoint claims, or where the graph structure is itself an explicit audit target.
   This protocol applies to countable, independently defined facts. It does not automatically
apply to semantic judgments such as code quality or whether a review was persuasive. A hash
requires equality or a cryptographic proof, not arithmetic in R. Safety properties such as “an
unapproved commit was never merged” require event ordering and authorization evidence; a zero
graph residual neither proves nor refutes them. Human intervention should follow provenance
and policy evidence, not an energy ratio or minimum-cut label.
   The prior web and native visualizers illustrate a graph and its derived values. They do not
constitute empirical validation. The prior “real-agent” scripts recorded self-reported scores and
Dirichlet disagreement. Those traces may motivate an interface, but they cannot be counted as
observations for the detector defined here. We preserve this distinction so that later real-data
collection can be judged against an explicit contract.

8  Related work and novelty boundary

Sparse recovery over graph incidence matrices already relates recovery conditions to graph
cycles and girth [1]; our cut-space support criterion is a dual, model-specific graph fact, not
a claimed new sparse-recovery theorem.  Combinatorial Hodge ranking already decomposes
pairwise edge data into gradient, curl, and harmonic parts and uses least squares to measure
cyclic inconsistency [2].  Discourse sheaves model selective communication, including lying,
with sheaf Laplacians [3]. Heterogeneous multi-agent coordination with cellular sheaves and
distributed optimization is developed by Hanks and colleagues [4]; learned sheaf-constrained
coordination appears in Sheaf-ADMM [5]. These sources rule out a general novelty claim for
sheaf-based multi-agent coordination, Hodge triage, or distributed repair.
   The narrower prospective contribution here is a domain-specific evaluation contract: exact
feature and watermark selection, provenance requirements, an independent truth oracle, and a
cheap-baseline cut gate for agent-workflow claims. The mathematics makes the limits of that
contract explicit. Whether an edge-only version has useful sensitivity or lower cost in a real
deployment remains open. We would treat a negative field result as a reason to ship ordinary
typed evidence checks instead.

9  Conclusion

Cycle consistency is a valid and efficiently decidable property of a selected set of edge reports. It
is not a certificate of truthful work, a causal diagnosis, a safety proof, or an optimal repair plan.
In the fully visible endpoint-packet setting, the duplicate-claim baseline catches every cycle
inconsistency and sometimes more. The near-term engineering result is a sharper observability
contract, a computable failure-separation margin for declared interventions, and a reproducible
falsification fixture. A claim of broad utility needs real evidence-grounded traces and a baseline
advantage that this model does not provide.

                                     Abstract

      A multi-agent workflow leaves local evidence on agents, handoffs, and joint review con-
       tracts. We model those observations as a typed cellular sheaf on a two-dimensional complex,
      with explicit vertex-to-edge and edge-to-face maps. The resulting degree-one cochains have
     two distinct algebraic obstructions: a violated face relation and a closed but nonexact class
       in H1. A relative connecting class tests whether a partially visible section can extend
      through unobserved contracts. We compute all three channels exactly on a heterogeneous
       four-role complex, including a face attachment that destroys H1 without changing total edge-
      compatibility detection. A sheaf edge-group distance characterizes when sparse erroneous
     handoffreports can be detected or uniquely recovered; a restricted projection gain quantifies
       stability. The graph-cycle case supplies a sharp baseline: when both endpoint claims are
       visible, direct equality catches every cycle inconsistency. These results specify what an audit
     can prove from selected evidence and what remains invisible, including coherent falsehood
     and copied observations. The prospective application is a provenance-bound audit of real
      agent workflows against independent ledger truth and equal-information contract checks;
       field utility and semantic fault attribution require that experiment.

1  Question and contribution

Agent workflows distribute evidence across roles: an author records work, a reviewer sees a
subset, a CI job observes a commit and test run, and a publisher sees an approval or artifact
receipt. A global claim can fail even when each observed overlap appears locally coherent.
The question is which incompatibilities can be inferred from the evidence an auditor actually
receives.
    Cellular sheaves give a precise language for this question. A stalk records one typed feature at
a cell; restriction maps state which part of a role’s state can be compared on a handoff or joint
contract. Cohomology distinguishes a local face-relation violation from a globally nontrivial
closed obstruction, while relative cohomology tests extension through a visibility boundary.
These constructions are established mathematics [2, 1, 6]. The contribution here is a concrete
agent-evidence contract, exact failure-observability criteria, and an executable comparison with
simpler checks. We make no claim that a topological signature alone establishes which agent
erred.
   The numerical examples use exact count features, one work item, and one immutable event-
log watermark. A production observation must bind each packet to its schema, work item,
source identity, log root, and evidence reference. An artifact digest or approval cannot be
treated as a real coordinate merely to make a Laplacian run. We keep the external truth oracle
separate from algebraic compatibility and use a synthetic fixture to expose the information
boundary before collecting field traces.

2.3  Partial observations and relative obstruction

An auditor may see only a subcomplex L ⊆K. The relative cochain complex C•(K, L; F)
consists of cochains that vanish on L. Standard relative sheaf cohomology supplies the exact
sequence [2]
              H0(K; F) −→H0(L; F|L) ∂−→H1(K, L; F) −→H1(K; F).

The connecting map is a coverage certificate for a visible compatible section; it does not ap-

problem.

Theorem 4 (Relative extension criterion). Let s ∈H0(L; F|L) be a section on the visible
subcomplex.  It extends to a global section on K  if and only  if ∂s = 0.  Vanishing proves
existence of a model-compatible extension, not uniqueness or agreement with unseen evidence.

Proof. Lift s to any vertex cochain es on K.  Its coboundary vanishes on L, so it is a relative
1-cocycle and ∂s = [Aes]. A different lift changes this class by a relative coboundary. If s has a
global-section lift, the class is zero. Conversely, if the class is zero, a relative vertex cochain z
satisfies Aes = Az; then es −z is a global section and still restricts to s.

Here B+ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The exact decision r = 0 needs no floating-point

Theorem 5 (Exact cycle test). For a complete integer observation on G, the following are
equivalent: (i) the reports are compatible; (ii) the oriented sum of y around every graph cycle
is zero; (iii) a spanning-forest propagation assigns integer potentials to vertices and every re-
maining edge agrees with its endpoint difference; and (iv) r(y) = 0. The dimension of the real
cycle space is |E| −|V | + c, where c is the number of connected components, including isolated
vertices.

Proof. If y = Bx, each cycle sum telescopes to zero. Choose one root per component, set its
potential to zero, and propagate along a spanning tree by adding or subtracting each oriented
edge value.  Every vertex receives an integer value. A non-tree edge closes a fundamental
cycle, so its agreement with the propagated difference is equivalent to that cycle sum being
zero. Fundamental cycles span the cycle space, proving the reverse implication. Orthogonal
decomposition gives RE = im B ⊕ker BT and hence the equivalence with r = 0.  Finally
rank B = |V | −c and rank-nullity yields dim ker BT = |E| −|V | + c.

then y = Bx by construction and the completion residual is identically zero. The graph Dirichlet
energy Pe ∥xu−xv∥2 may be positive for honest unequal counts; it is not the completion residual
in Eq. 5. Independent edge evidence is necessary for a nontrivial test.

4  What the algebra cannot identify

Theorem 6 (Information limits of compatibility). Under the model above: (a) on a forest, every
edge-difference vector is compatible; (b) adding any gradient Bz to a compatible observation
preserves compatibility, regardless of whether z is true; and (c) a jointly false but internally
consistent report passes the cycle test. A positive residual certifies incompatibility of the selected
reports, but alone identifies neither a dishonest party nor a physical network partition.

Proof. A forest has |E| = |V | −c, so Theorem 5 gives a zero-dimensional cycle space and
im B = RE.  If y = Bx, then y + Bz = B(x + z). In particular, x + z may disagree with an
independent event ledger while the residual remains zero. The same construction proves (c).
Permuting which packet is declared erroneous can produce the same nonzero cycle sum; the
algebra therefore supplies no unique source attribution.

  A three-edge triangle with values (1, 1, 1) around its orientation is incompatible because the
cycle sum is 3. A one-edge report with value 100 is always compatible: assign its endpoints
potentials 0 and 100. A triangle with values derived from false node values (10, 10, 10) is also
compatible. These examples distinguish a contradiction among reports from a contradiction
with the external event record.

5  The simpler baseline

When packets expose both endpoint claims, the auditor can compare repeated reports made
about the same node. Define D = 1 if some node has two incident packets giving it different
values at the same feature, work item, watermark, and log root. This check uses equality and
a map keyed by node; it needs no graph solver.

Theorem 7 (Duplicate-claim dominance for visible endpoints). On complete metadata-valid
packets as defined in Section 3,  if D = 0 then r(y) = 0.  Consequently, every positive cycle
residual is also detected by the duplicate-claim baseline. The converse need not hold: a duplicate
claim can be inconsistent even when the edge differences form a gradient.

Proof. If D = 0, choose xv to be the common endpoint claim for each non-isolated vertex v,
and choose any integer value for each isolated vertex. Then Eq. 4 gives ye = xv −xu on every
edge, so Theorem 5 yields r = 0. For the converse, take a triangle whose every reported edge
difference is zero.  Set endpoint claims to (0, 0) on two edges and (1, 1) on the third. The
differences are all zero, while at least one repeated node claim differs.

   This dominance result is a practical cut condition. With visible endpoint claims, topology
cannot improve detection recall over the equality baseline under the same metadata and packet
set.  It may still help explain a pattern when raw endpoint claims are unavailable, when only
edge differences can be disclosed, or when independent redundant paths have special provenance.
Those are distinct privacy and acquisition contracts requiring their own tests. We claim no cost
or utility advantage for the current setting.
